Settlement due to static load can be calculated relatively accurately, but movement caused by vibration, cavities, erosion and frost rarely can.
These effects have to be prevented by recognition, detailing and preventive measures.
Dynamic effects typically act for a long time with a constant magnitude.
They typically act for a short time, cyclically.
Saturated, uniformly graded fine sand is particularly sensitive to vibration.
Steeply graded, fine-grained soils are the most sensitive, especially when saturated.
Cohesive soils are more sensitive to vibration than loose sands.
Cohesive and coarse-grained soils are less sensitive.
If the excitation frequency falls within the resonance range, sudden, collapse-like settlement may occur.
Resonance – which is why the natural frequency of the soil mass must not coincide with the excitation frequency.
Vibrations during construction (piling, sheet piling) typically travel at most 20–30 m.
Within this zone of influence they also affect neighbouring buildings.
According to DIN 4150-3, the same vibration limit applies to residential and industrial buildings.
The short-term limit below 10 Hz is 5 mm/s for a residential building, 20 mm/s for an industrial building and 3 mm/s for a sensitive building.
Vibration can cause damage directly to the superstructure and also through compaction of the subsoil.
The second is often more dangerous: on loose sand even a small vibration causes permanent settlement.
The machine foundation must be rigidly connected to the floor of the building so that the vibration spreads out.
Quite the opposite: it must be separated by a movement joint so that the vibration does not pass on.
Around a pile driven into loose sand, the radius of the settlement crater is roughly 3D + L/2.
Compaction occurs in a zone of radius about 3D; the surface crater is much wider.
The focus (hypocentre) of an earthquake is at the surface and the epicentre is deep down.
The other way round: the hypocentre is deep down, and the epicentre is above it, at the surface.
The vast majority of earthquakes have a focal depth of at most 30 km.
Focal depth can range from a few km to 600–700 km, but most earthquakes are shallow.
An earthquake has a single intensity, which is the same everywhere.
It has one magnitude; the intensity differs from place to place and decreases with distance from the focus.
An increase of one unit of magnitude means about 32 times the energy.
10^1.5 ≈ 32; the amplitude is ten times larger.
EMS-98 determines the degree of intensity from the effects: on people, on objects and nature, and on buildings.
The scale has 12 degrees: I not felt … XII completely devastating.
Hungary has never had a damaging earthquake.
The earthquakes of Komárom (1763), Érmellék (1834), Kecskemét (1911), Dunaharaszti (1956) and Berhida (1985) all caused severe damage.
In the 1763 Komárom earthquake about a third of the town was destroyed.
Of the 1169 houses, 279 collapsed completely; the relatively small number of victims is explained by the light rammed-earth houses.
The design earthquake according to EC8 has a 10 % probability of exceedance in 50 years.
This corresponds to a return period of about 475 years; it is treated as an accidental action.
The reference peak ground acceleration in Hungary is between 0.5 and 1.0 g.
The Hungarian map gives values between 0.08 and 0.15 g.
The EC8 ground types are assigned on the basis of the shear wave velocity of the upper 30 m, the NSPT blow count and the shear strength cu.
There are seven types: A, B, C, D, E, S<sub>1</sub> and S<sub>2</sub>; in Hungary mainly C and D.
Soft ground damps the earthquake, so the shaking is less than on rock.
Soft ground amplifies the vibration (S = 1.35 for type D); in Mexico City the amplification was 4–5 times.
Liquefaction requires loose, saturated sand and cyclic shearing.
Because of the increased pore water pressure the effective stress drops to zero, and the soil loses its shear strength.
In Niigata in 1964 many houses tilted with their superstructure remaining intact.
The structure of about two thirds of the 340 tilted or settled RC buildings remained intact – the soil liquefied beneath the foundations.
Excavating a cavity does not change the original state of stress in the ground.
It does: the soil masses above and beside it move towards the cavity.
The deeper the cavity and the stronger the soil, the smaller and the later the displacement.
In deep, strong ground an arch forms above the cavity.
The rupture surface of the trough above a cavity runs at about 45° − φ/2 to the horizontal.
It runs up from the lower corner of the cavity to the surface at 45° + φ/2.
The magnitude of settlement above a cavity can be estimated from the soil mass squeezed into the cavity.
The volume of the surface trough is approximately equal to the volume of soil squeezed in.
There are more than 100 km of explored cellars beneath Eger.
130–150 km in Eger, 55–65 km beneath the centre of Pécs.
The tuff wall of a cellar keeps its strength even when soaked.
The strength of rhyodacite tuff drops to a third to a fifth when soaked – this is why the cavity must be kept dry.
At the inflection point of the Gaussian trough above a tunnel the surface is steepest.
Tilt and tensile strain are greatest here; a building located here is the most at risk.
During rapid drawdown the groundwater beneath the bank falls faster than the river level.
Slower: it stays higher, which is why a strong flow starts towards the river.
The critical hydraulic gradient for upward flow is about 1.
icr = γ′/γw ≈ 1: then the effective stress is zero and a boil forms.
Cloudy, sandy water pumped from a sump indicates that the soil is being drawn out too.
In quicksand this leads to cavities and significant settlement; filtered wells are needed.
The finer a filter layer, the better.
Two conditions are needed: it must retain the soil but also let water through freely (Terzaghi’s filter rule).
The most common cause of bridge collapses is scour of the piers.
According to an American survey, about 60 % of documented collapses.
Frost heave is caused mainly by the 9 % volume increase when water freezes.
The large heave is caused by ice lenses growing from the water supply.
Silt is more frost-susceptible than sandy gravel.
Silts belong to the most dangerous class (F4); clean gravel is not frost-susceptible.
In Hungarian practice the frost depth is generally 0.8 m.
For sand and gravel, with groundwater deeper than 2 m, 0.5 m; above 300 m above sea level 0.8 m and 1.0 m instead.
Beneath a poorly insulated cold store the ground can freeze to a depth of as much as 6–12 m.
The zero isotherm penetrates downwards until the heat flowing from the Earth’s interior makes up the loss.
To prevent frost beneath a cold store it is enough to thicken the reinforced concrete floor slab.
Thermal insulation and underfloor heating are needed; thicker concrete does not stop the frost.
Dynamic action
A load that changes suddenly or continuously over time, typically acting for a short time, cyclically (blasting, piling, traffic, earthquakes, wind gusts).
The frequency at which a system (soil mass, foundation, structure) responds to the smallest excitation with the largest amplitude.
Resonance
The excitation frequency falls within the resonance range; the amplitude is amplified, and collapse-like settlement may occur on loose soil.
Zone of influence
The distance to which the vibration of a source travels harmfully in the subsoil; for construction vibration typically 20–30 m.
Peak particle velocity
The maximum velocity of motion of the particles of the soil or the structure (mm/s); the main measure of vibration damage.
Machine foundation
A dynamically loaded foundation carrying machines; it is separated from the building by a movement joint, and the machine speed is detuned from the natural frequency.
Settlement crater
A funnel-shaped settlement forming around a driven pile because of soil compaction; its radius is roughly 3D + L/2.
Hypocentre (focus)
The point deep in the Earth where the rupture or slip of the rock begins.
Epicentre
The point on the surface above the focus.
The distance between the hypocentre and the epicentre; for the vast majority of earthquakes at most 30 km.
A logarithmic measure of the energy released at the focus; one unit ≈ 32 times the energy.
Intensity
The strength of the effect of the earthquake at a given place (MSK-64, EMS-98: 12 degrees).
Isoseismal
A line on the earthquake map connecting points of equal intensity.
P-wave, S-wave
The faster compressional (P) and the slower shear (S) wave; the distance to the focus can be calculated from the difference in their arrival times.
Reference peak ground acceleration
The basic design input according to EC8: a<sub>gR</sub> is the horizontal ground acceleration exceeded by an earthquake with a 10 % probability in 50 years; 0.08–0.15 g in Hungary.
Return period
The average time within which an earthquake of a given size occurs once. If the probability of exceedance is 10 % in 50 years, this is about 475 years.
The classification according to EC8 (A, B, C, D, E, S<sub>1</sub>, S<sub>2</sub>) on the basis of the shear wave velocity, N<sub>SPT</sub> value and c<sub>u</sub> of the upper 30 m.
The maximum acceleration of single-degree-of-freedom oscillators as a function of their natural period; its shape depends on the ground type.
In loose, saturated sand, cyclic shearing raises the pore water pressure to the effective stress, and the soil loses its shear strength.
Cavity excavation
Formation or failure of a tunnel, mine or cellar beneath existing structures; the ground moves towards the cavity.
Settlement trough
The settlement forming at the surface above a cavity or tunnel; its shape is well approximated by a Gaussian curve.
Rupture surface
The slip surface bounding the moving soil mass above a cavity; it runs up from the lower corner of the cavity at about 45° + φ/2.
The volume of the surface trough as a percentage of the tunnel cross-section; typically 0.3–0.5 % for modern shields.
Inflection point
The steepest point of the trough (x = i = K · z<sub>0</sub>); tilt and tensile strain are greatest here.
Backfilling
Filling a redundant cavity with fly-ash concrete, cement mortar or by grouting.
Undermined area
An area above working or abandoned mines, where the surface may settle for years.
Erosion by water
Flowing water tears away the fine grains of the soil, and cavities form under the foundations.
Rapid drawdown
The river level falls faster than the groundwater beneath the bank; a strong flow starts towards the river.
Hydraulic gradient
The fall in water level per unit length of flow path (i = Δh/L); the seepage force is proportional to it.
Critical gradient
i<sub>cr</sub> = γ′/γ<sub>w</sub> ≈ 1; for upward flow the effective stress is then zero and a boil forms.
Quicksand
Sand that has lost its bearing capacity because of upward-flowing water and behaves like a liquid.
Dewatering by pumping from a sump formed at the lowest point of the pit; in quicksand it may also draw out the soil.
Filter rule
Terzaghi’s conditions for the grain size of a filter layer: the filter must retain the protected soil and let water through freely.
Scour
The funnel dug into the bed by the vortex around a pier; if it reaches the foundation, the pier settles.
separate page
High-plasticity clay that swells when it takes up water and shrinks when it dries; it lifts and lowers a lightly loaded house in a seasonal cycle. In detail: Foundations on unfavourable ground ↗.
In-situ freezing
The pore water freezes in place; the volume increase of water of about 9 % gives only a small heave.
Ice lens
A horizontal ice layer growing from water flowing by capillarity to below the frost front; the cause of large frost heave.
Frost depth
The depth to which frost penetrates the ground; the foundation must go below it (generally 0.8 m in Hungary).
The sum of the daily mean temperatures of the frost period (°C·day); the main determinant of frost penetration.
Frost-susceptible soil
A soil in which ice lenses can form – mainly silts and very fine silty sands (F4).
Zero isotherm
The surface of points at 0 °C in the ground; beneath cold stores it can penetrate deeper year by year.
Underfloor heating (cold stores)
Heating pipes, cables or ventilation ducts placed below the thermal insulation, which keep the ground above freezing.
